title: Good Memorization, Bad Memorization
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane argues that 'memorization' is a polarising word in math teaching mainly because people rarely specify what should actually be memorised. He defines memorisation as knowing something without having to think about it, and argues its value lies specifically in small, widely applicable pieces of knowledge, like the difference between radius and diameter, that free up working memory for harder problems, not in narrow, single-use procedures like the quadratic formula, which he calls 'the opposite of the type of thing that's helpful to memorize.' He's careful to distinguish memorization-as-goal from drilling-as-method, advocating brief, spaced retrieval practice rather than repetitive drills. His larger point: teachers who fixate on debating whether to memorise big formulas overlook the small foundational knowledge that actually trips students up.
points: Kane defines memorisation precisely as 'knowing something without having to think about it,' distinct from the method used to get there -- spaced retrieval practice, not repetitive drilling.

He argues the real value of memorisation lies in small, widely transferable knowledge (radius vs. diameter, multiplication facts) that teachers overlook precisely because they've long since memorised it themselves.

He singles out narrow, single-use content like the quadratic formula as 'the opposite of the type of thing that's helpful to memorize,' arguing debates over such formulas distract from the smaller pieces that matter more.

His classroom method is a five-question spaced-retrieval Do Now, each question recurring at increasing intervals, taking under five minutes daily and freeing the rest of class for harder problem-solving.
quotes: To me, memorization means knowing something without having to think about it. My goal as a teacher is to pick out all the little pieces of knowledge that my students need when they're solving complex problems.

Memorization is powerful when that knowledge is useful in lots of different places; memorizing something that’s only useful in a narrow context isn’t a good use of time and probably isn’t going to stick anyway.
Teachers forget about them because we have them memorized, so we don't have to think about them! Walk into a typical 7th grade class that's learning about circles.
The quadratic formula is the opposite of the type of thing that's helpful to memorize.

I give a quick five-question retrieval practice Do Now at the start of each class for students to practice stuff I want them to memorize. Each question comes up a bunch of times at increasing intervals.
